newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania on track for $100m World Bank loan.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania on track for $100m World Bank loan.

text.p: Tanzania is on target for a World Bank loan of up to $100 million which could be granted by early 1997, a World Bank official said on Tuesday.
But World Bank Tanzania representative Ron Brigish said reports in the local media here that a Structural Adjustment Credit (SAC) had already been agreed were premature.
"As far as we're (World Bank) concerned we'll be appraising a structural adjustment credit in November and we hope we can take it to our board in early 1997," he told Reuters.
"We think this government is much more committed to fiscal stability than the previous one," Brigish added.
President Benjamin Mkapa won elections last October and has pledged a commitment to reforms and reduction of corruption.
Brigish said the World Bank was closely watching that the Tanzanian government stuck to its June budget forecasts.
"This is one of the tests. The government has come to agreements before with the IMF (International Monetary Fund) and then gone off track," said Brigish.
Tanzania last drew credit from the IMF in 1992.
Brigish said that Tanzania, one of the world's poorest, could receive between $80-100 million Bank financial support.
"We will be looking at a fair injection of balance of payments support which Tanzania needs," he said.
Latest statistics from the central Bank of Tanzania show the country's foreign debt as currently about $7.5 billion.

Following the November appraisal of the government's financial requirements, negotiations would open with the Tanzania government and a formal proposal would then be put to the board of the World Bank.

"We'll appraise in November -- we're almost there," said Brigish. Asked to assess the current prospects of a World Bank soft loan, he said: "I'm fairly confident given the commitment of this government to economic reform and the leadership of President Mkapa in this respect."

The IMF has said Tanzania could receive an Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) worth $234 million by this month with further debt relief to follow from the Paris Club worth more than $200 million.
Restoration of IMF credit will trigger an estimated $1.2 billion in donor bilateral aid, economic experts said.

Brigish said key areas of World Bank concern about Tanzania included a slowdown in public sector reforms including further cuts to the civil service and privatisation of parastatals. Improvement in revenue collection and a elimination of official corruption were other areas of concern, Brigish said.
A report of a parliamentary investigation last month said Finance Minister Simon Mbilinyi acted improperly over imports of cooking oil and should be "taken to task".
The report said Mbilinyi ignored advice from his ministry officials who said the oil should not receive tax exemption.
President Mkapa has made no comment on the report.
